title: Packaging you can actually open — Image Wiki
text:
Packaging you can actually open
  The point where packaging graphics meet hands and eyes — opening force, tactile cues, contrast on a curved glossy surface, and the barcode rules designers usually meet only after the print run.

  
    Termaccessible packaging / inclusive packaging design
    Also calledinclusive packaging, accessible packaging, opening forces, frustration-free packaging
    Not the same aschild-resistant packaging, tamper evidence, sustainable packaging
    Read8 min
  

  
    
      On this page
      
        The numbers are hands, not opinionsStructure is where most of it happensCues you can find with your fingersContrast, on a curved, glossy, moving surfaceThe constraint you discover after the print runCommon mistakes
      
    
  

  Think of the last time you attacked a blister pack with kitchen scissors, or gave up on a shrink-wrapped box and used your teeth. The graphics on that package may have been beautiful. It still failed, at the only moment that was not optional.
A pack has to be found on a shelf (Packaging hierarchy), and then gripped, twisted, torn and emptied by a specific pair of hands — some of them arthritic, one-handed, shaking, or busy holding a baby.
The numbers are hands, not opinions
Microsoft's packaging team publishes a checklist with thresholds on it, which is more than most people in this field commit to.



Microsoft Packaging & Content Design, Creating Accessible Packaging: An Inclusive Design Toolkit, Spring 2026, page 30. © Microsoft, CC BY-NC-ND. Reproduced whole and unmodified.
Zoom in on the middle column, because it is the part designers never see written down. Opening must not need a force of operation over 3 lb (1.36 kg). The pack must open with one hand, and without the ability to pinch, to twist the wrist, or to grasp with the hand — three separate abilities, tested separately. Boxes over 5 lb must allow two hands. A graspable area must be no wider than 3 inches. No tools. If opening takes several actions, they must be performable one at a time.
Then read the two rules that sit in the left column as if they were graphics rules, because they are: text and graphics at a contrast ratio of at least 3:1, and colour never the only carrier of meaning.


This is not an edge case. Roughly 1.3 billion people, or 16% of the world's population, experience significant disability; among adults it is closer to 1 in 4; and once you count temporary and situational disability — a broken wrist, carrying an infant — as many as 83% of us will experience disability while of working age (PACK-001, page 9).
The framing that makes this useful is in the same guide: disability is not a health condition but "a mismatch between a person and their environment. As such, disability is designed." A jar needing a strong wrist has designed a disability into itself. And solve for one, extend to many is why this is not charity work: a pack that opens one-handed for someone with one arm opens one-handed for someone holding a phone.
Structure is where most of it happens



Microsoft Packaging & Content Design, Creating Accessible Packaging: An Inclusive Design Toolkit, Spring 2026, page 16. © Microsoft, CC BY-NC-ND. Reproduced whole and unmodified.
A pull tab drawn as an engineering part: units mm, scale 100%, six variants from 16.5 × 18 mm up to 36 × 30 mm, each with its corner radius called out (r7.5, r9, r18). The dark slot in the middle of every tab is a tactile element, not decoration.
The four guidance notes are the mechanism. Size the tab based on the effort needed to lift — force determines size, not the layout. Leave space around the tab for access, because a tab flush against a wall cannot be pinched. Adjust radius for strength, because a tight corner is where the card tears. And concentric alignment of tabs with wayfinding iconography — the printed arrow and the physical tab must share a centre, or the finger goes to the wrong place.


Two principles there matter more than the dimensions. Simple is best: "more simple steps are easier than fewer complicated steps", which overturns the old three-steps-to-product target — a clever fold that halves the step count can double the dexterity needed. And reduce pivot points: every lift-then-rotate-then-pull sheds users.
Cues you can find with your fingers
Tactile detail is cheap and specific. Microsoft targets a relief height of 0.2 mm from spot UV varnish or an emboss, extending the UV area 0.5 mm beyond the artwork to absorb print registration tolerance (PACK-002, page 11). Braille does not scale with the pack: dot diameter 1.5 mm, dot spacing 2.4 mm centre to centre, character pitch 6 mm, kept 8 mm clear of any edge or crease, always reading left to right in the box's own orientation. Their research puts optimal braille height at 0.4–0.5 mm, though they admit shipping 0.2 mm, "less than recommended" (PACK-001, pages 58–60).
The neat trick is braille used as a pointer rather than as text: a few raised dots beside a QR code, telling a blind user something worth scanning is here even if they do not read braille. On QR codes the guide is plain — there is no standard size, so test from a printed sample, not on screen.
Contrast, on a curved, glossy, moving surface
The honest part is in Microsoft's own footnote: there are no recognised standards for print contrast ratios equivalent to WCAG, and no agreed formula for measuring it. So they measure 3:1 from the digital source file and warn that "different inks and substrates will combine to affect the final appearance when printed" (PACK-002, page 31). Treat any on-pack contrast figure as a design-file number, not a measurement of the object.
The rest of their typographic advice is unglamorous and correct: sans-serif with a large x-height, line length under 60 characters, left-aligned, leading up to 150%, no hyphenation. Icons have a minimum size — and the two documents disagree, 6 mm in the 2025 guide and 5 mm in the 2026 toolkit, which makes it a working number rather than a law. About 4.5% of people have some form of colour blindness, so a symbol needs a second channel: a text label, or a different shape.
The constraint you discover after the print run
Everything above is negotiable with a stakeholder. The barcode is not: a machine grades it.

462001745555411 X7 XX = the narrowest barQuiet zones kept clearscans first time, every orientationart4620017455554left quiet zone goneArtwork pushed into the quiet zonesame 95 modules, same size, will not scanreal EAN-13 for GTIN 4620017455554

The same 95 modules, printed at the same size, twice. X is the width of the narrowest bar, and every other dimension in the symbol is a multiple of it — including the blank quiet zones, which for EAN-13 must be at least 11X on the left and 7X on the right.
On the right, a designer has run a coloured panel up to the first bar. Nothing about the code changed, and the scanner now has no way to tell where the symbol begins. This is the single most common artwork error in packaging, and it survives every visual review because it looks fine.


GS1's ten-step guide holds the rest of the trap (PACK-009). Bars must be a single dark colour — black, dark blue, dark brown, dark green — on a light background, which is often just the substrate. Never red, orange, pink or light yellow bars: most scanners use a red light source, and under red light those colours vanish. Truncating an EAN/UPC symbol to save vertical space is not permitted, because retail scanners read omnidirectionally and need the height. Placement must survive the packing line — not over a carton edge, under a fold, beneath a flap. And print quality is graded to ISO/IEC 15416 (linear) and 15415 (2D), with GS1 setting the minimum grade, verifier aperture and wavelength per application; a verifier "looks at the symbol in the way a scanner does but goes further by grading the symbol's quality".



Sokolikmawwer0, EAN-13 barcode on a gummy candy package, 2026. Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0.
What a graded symbol looks like from a millimetre away. The bars are dark navy, not black, which GS1 permits, and the light background reads as the plain film rather than a printed white panel.
Now look at the bar edges. They are soft and slightly wavy, and the wide bars have spread into the spaces — ink gain, the normal behaviour of ink on flexible film. Edge sharpness and bar width are exactly what a verifier measures, which is why printers specify a bar width reduction in the artwork, shaving the bars so the printed result lands on target. The human-readable line carries all 13 digits, as EAN-13 requires; if the bars degrade past grading, that line is the fallback at the till.


Common mistakes

"Accessible means ugly." Microsoft's answer: do not be tempted to believe adequate contrast means a less premium experience.
"We tested it, so it works." Their guides insist on co-design with disabled participants from the start, and that no empathy exercise substitutes for it. Testing at the end is not testing.
"Fewer opening steps is better." Only if each step stays simple. Fewer, cleverer steps are usually worse.
"The barcode is prepress's problem." Quiet zone, colour, size and placement are artwork decisions, made months before anyone scans anything.
"Braille scales with the pack." It does not. Dot size and spacing are fixed whatever the pack.

A tactile emboss and a barcode quiet zone both look perfect in a PDF. One is judged by a fingertip and the other by a red laser, and neither cares what your monitor showed you.

Checking a pack for access, in five moves

Open it with one hand only. Then again without pinching. Then without twisting your wrist.
Find the intended entry point without reading anything. Is there a tab, loop or notch you can feel?
Hold a printed sample at arm's length in poor light. Does the variant name still separate?
Does colour alone carry functional information? If so, it is missing for colour-blind readers.
Put a straight edge beside the barcode: clear space on both sides, wider on the left?



  
    
      Read next
      
        
          
            
              Packaging hierarchy
              Ordering what a pack says, under constraints no other graphic design job has — a reader who is standing up, holding it, deciding in seconds, from a metre away, next to fifty rivals, with part of the layout dictated by law.
            
          
        
          
            
              Contrast
              Difference — how much a part of a picture differs from what sits next to it. An edge exists only where something changes, so contrast is what makes anything visible at all.
            
          
        
          
            
              Legibility and readability
              Two different measurements that get treated as one — whether you can tell the characters apart, and whether you can get through a paragraph without effort.
            
          
        
          
            
              Sign legibility is arithmetic
              How big, how thick, how far apart, how much contrast. Most of it is calculated from viewing distance and mounting height, and the legal numbers are floors rather than goals.
